newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Leukaemia survivors risk obesity, researchers say.
newsitem.headline: Leukaemia survivors risk obesity, researchers say.

text.p: Children who survive leukaemia have a very high risk of becoming obese as adults, possibly because they exercise less than their healthy counterparts, British doctors said on Friday.
Dr John Reilly of the University of Glasgow and colleagues found children who had survived acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) often gained too much weight.

"Children who have ALL typically gain more weight than they should during the two years they spend on chemotherapy, and continue to gain excess weight after treatment is completed," he told the Eighth European Congress on Obesity in Dublin.
"A very high proportion of long-term survivors are obese."
Tests indicated the children who had survived leukaemia exercised less, said Reilly, a physiologist.

He tested the metabolic rates of 15 overweight leukaemia survivors and compared them to 15 healthy children matched by age, gender and other factors. The children who had not had cancer had higher metabolic rates.

This could be because they exercised more -- Reilly said he had to check this. But he said resting metabolic rates, a measure of overall metabolism, indicated the children who had been ill did not have an overall physiological probem and they did not eat more.
He said doctors should encourage leukaemia survivors -- and more than 75 percent of children with ALL now survive -- to be more active.
